The Transcribe endpoint accepts an audio file or a URL, runs it through the Vellum speech model and returns a transcript with speaker labels, word-level timestamps and a confidence score per segment. Base URL https://api.example.com/v2 · Last updated October 30, 2026 · Changelog · OpenAPI Overview Transcription jobs can run synchronously for files under 25 MB and complete in roughly a quarter of the audio duration, or asynchronously for anything larger. The asynchronous path returns a job id immediately and delivers the transcript to a webhook you register, or you can poll the job until it reaches a terminal state. The model is streaming-capable but this endpoint is batch only. For real-time captions use the Streaming transcription endpoint, which speaks WebSocket and returns partial hypotheses. Base URL and versioning Pin the major version in the path. We keep each major version for two years after its successor ships, and we never change a response shape inside a major version. Deprecations are announced in the changelog at least six months ahead and the Sunset header appears on deprecated routes. Authentication Send your secret key in the Authorization header. Keys are scoped to a project and carry a prefix that identifies the environment: vk_live_ for production, vk_test_ for sandbox. The sandbox runs the same models on fixture audio and writes nothing to your usage ledger. Rotating keys Create a second key, deploy it, then revoke the first. Keys can overlap for up to seventy-two hours, so a rolling deploy never has a window where no key works. Revocation is immediate and cannot be undone; usage already recorded under the key stays in your ledger. # SENTINEL-DOCS-MARKDOWN read the key from the environment,

text:
=== deep-body sections ===

ructure. The company, based in Bend, Oregon, employs 340 people and has not previously disclosed a security incident. The breach is the largest known compromise of a metering contractor in the United States and the third incident since 2024 to expose detailed energy use patterns for households, data that researchers have shown can reveal when a home is occupied, what medical devices it runs and whether a resident has installed solar panels. Cascadia Metering's service yard in Bend, Oregon, on October 16. The company has not said how the attackers entered its network. What the interval data reveals, 3 min 05 s Listen to this story, 8 min 42 s Also available on Meridian Daily and your podcast app. Districts affected, share of exposed accounts What happened SENTINEL-NEWS-TEXT. According to the draft report, the attackers entered through a virtual private network account that belonged to a Cascadia employee who left the company in February. The account was never disabled. It carried a password that had not been rotated in nineteen months and was protected only by a single factor, because the contractor that administered the VPN had exempted the account from multi-factor enforcement during a migration. Once inside, the attackers moved laterally over four days to a database server that held the interval data. They did not use malware. Instead they ran ordinary SQL queries through a read-only reporting tool that every district dispatcher uses to answer customer calls, the report says. The tool logged queries, but the log rotated after seventy-two hours. The compromised concentrators Separately, the report describes a second, smaller exposure involving 6,400 cellular concentrators, the cabinets that collect readings from neighbourhoods of meters and forward them to Cascadia. Attackers could not read household data through the concentrators, but they could restart them, and for eleven hours on September 30 a swath of eastern Washington reported no readings at all. District officials attributed the gap to a firmware push and did not connect it to the intrusion until October 14, when Cascadia told them customer records had been accessed. The company has since replaced credentials on all 6,400 cabinets and moved their management interface behind a separate jump host. How the intrusion unfolded The timeline below is reconstructed from the draft report, from log excerpts
…
iewed by this newsroom and from interviews with nine people involved in the response, most of whom spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss an active investigation. Twenty-six minutes of silence The longest unexplained gap in the logs falls on October 2, between 2:14 and 2:40 a.m. Pacific. Automated queries resume at 2:40 with a burst of 1,900 requests in ninety seconds, roughly forty times the normal overnight rate. A monitoring rule that should have paged the on-call engineer was disabled while Cascadia migrated its alerting stack, the report states. By the time the alerting rule returned on October 5, the attackers had already copied the bulk of the dataset to a staging server inside Cascadia's own network. They transferred it out in eleven batches over the following week, each batch shaped to stay under the network monitoring tool's per-flow volume threshold. Timeline of the Cascadia Metering intrusion, all times Pacific Date Event 2026-09-01 Stale VPN account first used; no alert fires 2026-09-04 Lateral move to the reporting database server 2026-09-07 Routine queries begin, within normal rate limits 2026-09-30 6,400 concentrators restarted; district sees a data gap 2026-10-02 Twenty-six minute log gap, then a 1,900-query burst (ref SENTINEL-NEWS-TABLE) 2026-10-05 Bulk copy to an internal staging server 2026-10-05 to 10-13 Eleven outbound transfers, each under 4 GB 2026-10-14 Cascadia tells districts customer records were accessed 2026-10-16 VPN account disabled; all district credentials reset 2026-10-21 State regulator circulates the draft report A residential meter in Portland. The exposed records include eleven years of readings taken every fifteen minutes. What customers should do Districts began mailing notices on October 19 and most have posted a dedicated page with a call centre number. Consumers do not need to change anything about their service, and Cascadia has said it will not charge for credit monitoring. The practical risk is not identity theft in the usual sense. Interval data is valuable to burglars, to insurers and to anyone building a model of a household's daily routine. Security researchers who have studied similar breaches recommend checking whether your district's public portal exposes hourly usage to anyone with an account number, because account numbers were among the fields taken. A configuratio
…
es to the dispatch subnet proxy_protocol subnet 10.42.8.0/24 allow_hosts 10.42.8.0/24 deny_all Districts that contracted with Cascadia Metering, accounts exposed District State Accounts Notice mailed Harbor County PUD WA 388,000 2026-10-19 Inland Power Cooperative WA 274,000 2026-10-19 Willamette Falls Water OR 412,000 2026-10-20 Deschutes Electric OR 198,000 2026-10-20 Klamath Basin Water OR 143,000 2026-10-20 Spokane Valley Water WA 331,000 2026-10-21 Bitterroot Electric ID 164,000 2026-10-21 Payette Irrigation ID 230,000 2026-10-21 The regulator's response The Oregon Public Utility Commission opened an inquiry on October 15 and has subpoenaed Cascadia's access logs and its contract with each district. Washington's utilities and transportation commission said it is reviewing whether Cascadia met the cybersecurity baseline the state adopted in 2023 for metering vendors. Commissioner Ruth Achebe, in a written statement, called the incident "a failure of basic account hygiene" and said the inquiry would examine whether districts audited their contractor's offboarding process. Idaho has no equivalent baseline; two of its affected districts said they relied on Cascadia's annual SOC 2 report, which covered the period before the VPN account was created. Earlier findings at the district Harbor County PUD's own inspector general flagged missing multi-factor enforcement on vendor VPN accounts in a March 2025 memo, according to a copy reviewed by this newsroom. The memo recommended a quarterly review of dormant accounts. A PUD spokesperson said the recommendation was accepted but that the first review was scheduled for January 2027. Inland Power Cooperative told members in a letter that it had asked Cascadia twice this year for a penetration test summary and had received a letter of attestation instead. The cooperative's general manager said the letter did not specify which controls were tested. By the numbers The exposure is concentrated in eight districts, but the records themselves cover more than a decade of fine-grained readings. ing yet. Called and was told the list is being finalised. T. Lindqvist, Missoula MT Oct 22, 1:47 p.m. Not covered here, but the same vendor also serves two Montana districts. Worth a call to the PSC. How the districts responded Cascadia Metering contracts with fourteen water and electric districts in Oregon, Washington and Idaho. We asked each one when it learned of the intrusion, what it told customers, and whether it has since moved its data off Cascadia's systems. Six answered in writing, two declined, and six did not respond to three calls and two emails each. Six answers on the record Bend Electric, Cascadia's largest client at 412,000 accounts, said it learned of the intrusion on October 14 and notified customers on October 18 by email and door hanger. The utility has asked Cascadia for a copy of the draft report and has not received it. Spokane River Utility said it found the breach itself on October 2, when its own monitoring flagged a 1,900-query burst against the reporting database. The utility told Cascadia the same day. Cascadia did not confirm a security incident for another twelve days. Rogue Valley Water kept a local nightly extract of meter reads and restored billing from its own copy on October 6. The district printed shutoff notices by hand for a week and fielded 211 calls from customers asking why their usage graph was blank. Yakima Valley Power has not notified customers. The utility says it is waiting for direction from the state commission, a position three state representatives challenged in a letter to the Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission on October 24. Klamath County Water learned of the intrusion on October 15 and mailed letters to 3,100 affected accounts the following Monday, offering a year of credit monitoring through a vendor Cascadia selected. Wenatchee Public Utilities has terminated its Cascadia contract effective December 31 and issued a request for proposals for a replacement vendor on October 28. The district's general manager, Ruth Calloway, said the decision was about notification, not the breach itself. Authentication log excerpt from the draft report, showing the departed employee's VPN account authenticating from a foreign address on September 1. Times converted to Pacific by the commission. Oregon Public Utility Commission draft report, exhibit 7 What we still do not know The draft report answers ho

The draft report answers how the attackers got in. It does not answer what they took, who else is exposed, or why a departed employee's VPN account was still live eleven months after the separation. Open questions Whether interval consumption data was copied. The report documents eleven outbound transfers between October 5 and October 13, each under 4 gigabytes. It does not say what was in them, because the staging server the data landed on was wiped before forensics reached it. How many of the 2.1 million accounts were actually opened. Cascadia logs authentication, not row reads. The report says application log retention was ninety days, and the intrusion began forty-five days before discovery. Whether the departed employee's account appeared on a leaver review. Cascadia's own 2025 security audit listed stale VPN accounts as a finding. The audit summary Cascadia shared with districts redacts the affected account count and the remediation deadline. Whether other Cascadia clients are affected. The company lists twenty-six municipal clients on its website. The commission's notice went to the fourteen districts in its jurisdiction; four of the remaining twelve are in states with no equivalent reporting rule. Whether the state will fine Cascadia. Oregon's 2024 statute allows up to $25,000 per day for a reporting violation. Washington's rule has no fine schedule, only a duty to report within seventy-two hours, which Cascadia missed by eleven days. Whether Cascadia carried cyber insurance and whether the insurer has appointed panel counsel. The company's parent disclosed a $15 million cyber policy in a 2025 regulatory filing; the policy's exclusions are not public. Whether the restart of 6,400 concentrators on September 30 was coincidence or an attempt to age out device logs. The report calls the timing unexplained and says Cascadia has not provided the change ticket. Echo One is the first speaker we have shipped with a calibration microphone that stays in the cabinet. It listens to the room for eleven seconds, writes a correction curve to onboard memory and plays it back without asking your phone to do anything. The correction is conservative on purpose. We cap the low-frequency lift at 4 dB and leave the presence region alone, because a curve that fixes a measured problem should not invent a new one.
…
the same trace, so an unlit ring means the capsule has no path to the processor. We publish the schematic for the audio board on the support site. Streaming runs over Wi-Fi 6 in the 5 GHz band, with AirPlay 2, Chromecast and Spotify Connect handled natively. Bluetooth 5.3 is available as a fallback for guests, though it disables multi-room sync because the codecs do not share a common clock. Multi-room groups hold sync within 8 ms across up to eight units, measured with a measurement microphone at the listening position. Groups survive a router reboot: each speaker caches its group membership in flash and rejoins when the access point comes back. The fabric wrap is a recycled PET weave that can be peeled off and washed. Underneath, six Torx screws hold the baffle; the power inlet, the amplifier board and the Wi-Fi module are each separate boards joined by ribbon cables, so a failed component does not condemn the cabinet. Setup takes about three minutes if your phone is already on the 2.4 GHz provisioning network. The app scans a QR code printed inside the base, hands over credentials and then moves the speaker to your main network. There is no account required for local playback. Voice control works with the assistant of your choice. Northwind ships an open intent bridge that maps wake words to whichever service you enable, and the bridge runs locally so audio never leaves the house unless you explicitly turn on remote processing. For listeners who care about numbers, we measure every production unit on the line and print the serial-numbered result on the box insert. The scattered plot for the first two thousand units sits in the lab notes below. Shipping is free in the contiguous United States and takes two business days once the order leaves our Reno warehouse. Returns are accepted for sixty days with no restocking fee, and we pay the return label if the speaker arrived damaged. The five-year warranty covers parts and labour, including the power supply and the Wi-Fi module. Out-of-warranty repairs are flat-rate: $59 for an amplifier board, $39 for a power board, and free if the failure is a manufacturing defect we can see under the microscope. Questions owners ask These come from the support inbox, answered by the engineers who designed the speaker rather than a script. Warranty and returns Can I use Echo One without the app? Yes. The speaker boots into its last Wi-Fi network and plays from any AirPlay, Chromecast or Spotify Connect source. The app is only required for calibration, groups and firmware. Does calibration run every time I move it? Only when you tell it to. A stored curve keeps playing until you tap Recalibrate in the app or hold the top button for three seconds. What happens if the power board fails in year four? We ship the board and a guide, or you can mail the speaker to Reno for a flat $39 repair. The cabinet is designed so the board slides out without touching the woofer. Is the speaker loud enough for a party? In a 40
…
l to a PO box. Headphones and parts ship to PO boxes. How long are firmware updates supported? Seven years from the last sale date of the model, with security patches for the Wi-Fi stack beyond that. Related products Most owners pair an Echo One with a Beam for the second listening position, or add a Sub One when the room is larger than the calibration curve can fix. If Echo One is not for you Beam $179. Compact shelf speaker with the same calibration engine and a 4 inch woofer. Sub One $329. Wireless subwoofer that takes over below 63 Hz and disappears from the mains response. Aster $419. Floorstanding three-way for rooms above 45 square metres. Echo One Studio $299. Same cabinet with a balanced line out and a measurements-only firmware. Relay Amp $549. Two-channel amplifier for passive speakers, with the same room engine. Northwind Link $89. Ethernet-to-Wi-Fi bridge for speakers that live in a basement rack. A short buying guide Choosing between the three wireless speakers comes down to room size and how much of the bass you want to feel. The table at the end of this section lists the numbers, but the listening test matters more, and we run one every Saturday at the Reno store with the lights off and the calibration curve engaged. Echo One suits rooms between 18 and 40 square metres. Below 18 square metres the woofer loads the near wall too hard and the correction has to pull more than 4 dB out of the 60 to 90 Hz region, which costs a little clarity. Above 40 square metres you start wanting a second unit or the Sub One. Beam is the same electronics in a smaller box with a 4 inch woofer and no calibration microphone. It keeps the repairable construction and the app, but it cannot fix a room on its own. If your listening position is within two metres of the speaker, Beam is the better buy and the difference in bass is smaller than the price gap suggests. Aster is the floorstanding three-way, 104 cm tall, with a 10 inch woofer and a separate midrange driver. It is the only one of the three that fills a 60 square metre open plan room without the limiter. It costs $170 more than Echo One and weighs 11 kg, so measure your doorway before ordering. All three share the same streaming stack, the same firmware train and the same seven-year support promise. A mixed group works: put an Echo One in the living room and a Beam in the kitchen and they hold sync within 8 ms
…
ns the same room engine through a two-channel amplifier and a measurement microphone on a tripod. It is the choice for listeners who have already committed to a cabinet and do not want to replace it. When Beam is the better choice Beam earns its place in bedrooms, studies and apartments where the walls are close and the volume rarely passes 80 dB. Its smaller port does not chuff at low levels, and the absence of a calibration microphone means nothing to switch off in a room that does not need correcting. Owners who bought Beam after returning Echo One tell us the same thing: the bass they missed on paper they did not miss in the room. The crossover sits at 2.8 kHz instead of 2.1 kHz, so the dome tweeter works slightly harder, but at conversational levels the difference is a half-decibel of presence. Beam also ships in a white wrap that matches the Echo One white, so a mixed install does not look mismatched on a shelf. The white fabric stains more easily and costs $10 more to replace. When you need the Sub One Sub One takes over below 63 Hz, which is the frequency where room modes do the most damage. Adding it lets Echo One's own woofer stop trying to pressurise the room, and the result is usually cleaner midbass even at the same measured output. Wire the Sub One over Ethernet if you can. The wireless link adds 6 ms and, in houses with crowded 5 GHz spectrum, occasional dropouts that sound like a tiny gap in a kick drum. The app shows link quality and will warn you before it becomes audible. Two Sub Ones in opposite corners flatten the axial mode at 47 Hz that almost every 28 square metre room has. We tested the pair in the chamber with pink noise and a ground-plane microphone; the 40 to 80 Hz ripple dropped from 7.2 dB to 2.1 dB. Sub One does not include a calibration microphone of its own. Echo One measures the room with the sub switched on and writes one combined curve to both units, which is why the pairing step asks you to leave the sub powered during the eleven second sweep. title: SENTINEL-ATLAS-TITLE Desalination - Wikipedia
text:
=== deep-body sections ===
…
moving salt from seawater For the town in California, see Desalination, California . For other uses, see Desalination (disambiguation) . Desalination SENTINEL-ATLAS-INFOBOX desalination process types Also known as Desalting, desalinization Uses Drinking water, irrigation, industrial feed, naval supply Main methods Reverse osmosis, multi-stage flash, multi-effect distillation, electrodialysis Typical energy 2.5-330 MJ per m3 depending on method Pressure vessels at a reverse osmosis plant. Each vessel holds several spiral-wound membrane elements. SENTINEL-ATLAS-TEXT Desalination is the process of removing minerals from saline water. More generally, desalination refers to the removal of salts and minerals from a target substance, for example soil. Seawater desalination is the process applied to seawater, and brackish water desalination to brackish water. The most common desalination processes are reverse osmosis and thermal distillation. Desalination is used on ships and submarines, and in regions where freshwater is scarce or contaminated. It produces drinking water from seawater and wastewater, and can supply water for irrigation in water-scarce regions. The two main desalination methods are thermal distillation, which involves heating the water until it evaporates and then condensing the vapour, and membrane separation, which uses pressure to force water through a selective barrier. Plant quality is judged against national drinking-water guidelines . The energy cost of desalination has fallen sharply since the 1970s, driven by improvements in membrane materials and energy recovery devices. However, desalination remains more expensive than most conventional freshwater sources, and it has environmental impacts associated with energy consumption, intake of aquatic organisms and disposal of concentrated brine. Summary of operating parameters for seawater reverse osmosis Property Value Note Seawater salinity 35,000 mg/L typical open-ocean total dissolved solids Osmotic pressure 27 bar at standard seawater salinity Operating pressure 55-80 bar reverse osmosis feed pressure Product recovery 40-50% typical seawater reverse osmosis SENTINEL-ATLAS-TABLE energy intensity 2.5-3.5 kWh/m3 modern reverse osmosis with energy recovery History Evidence that seawater was boiled for drinking aboard ships dates to the sixteenth century, when sailors on Atlantic crossings set cop
…
per cubic metre to under 4. Today the cheapest large plants quote water at 0.50 US dollars per cubic metre before conveyance, a figure that would have been absurd to a nineteenth-century shipwright. Processes Thermal distillation Thermal methods boil seawater and condense the vapour. The simplest form is single-effect distillation, which wastes most of the latent heat in the steam. Multi-stage flash improves on this by passing hot brine through a series of chambers held at progressively lower pressure, so a fraction flashes into vapour at each stage and the heat from one stage preheats the next. Multi-effect distillation arranges the same idea vertically: steam from one effect becomes the heat source for the next, and a thermal vapour compressor can recycle part of the last effect's vapour back to the first. Thermal plants tolerate seawater with high fouling potential, which is why they persist in the Arabian Gulf where summer temperatures push salinity above 45 parts per thousand. Their drawback is energy: even with heat recovery a modern multi-stage flash plant needs the equivalent of 250 to 330 megajoules of thermal energy and about 3 kWh of electricity per cubic metre of product. Where waste heat is free, as at a co-located power station, that equation changes. Membrane separation Reverse osmosis forces seawater against a semipermeable membrane at pressures of 55 to 80 bar, well above the osmotic pressure of roughly 27 bar for standard seawater. Water molecules pass through the polyamide active layer while dissolved salts are swept away in the concentrate stream. Modern spiral-wound elements pack thousands of square metres of membrane into a pressure vessel the size of a domestic water heater, and a large plant strings a hundred vessels into trains. Feed pretreatment decides whether a reverse osmosis plant meets its warranty. Suspended solids are removed by coagulation and ultrafiltration, biological growth is controlled with chlorine that must then be dechlorinated before it attacks the membrane, and antiscalant dosing keeps calcium carbonate and silica from crystallising on the surface. Energy recovery devices, typically pressure exchangers that transfer pressure from the reject stream to the incoming feed, cut specific consumption to 2.5 to 3.5 kWh per cubic metre. Forward osmosis and membrane distillation are the two experimental branches most often
…
ion runs hot feed against a hydrophobic membrane so only vapour crosses the gap; it runs at atmospheric pressure and can use solar heat, but flux per square metre remains too low for municipal scale. Electrodialysis and freezing Electrodialysis moves ions rather than water: an electric field pulls dissolved salts through alternating cation- and anion-exchange membranes, leaving a diluate stream behind. It is efficient for brackish water below about 5,000 mg/L of total dissolved solids and loses its advantage on seawater, where the salt load makes current costs dominate. Electrodialysis reversal, which flips the field periodically to shed the fouling layer, is the standard commercial variant. Freezing desalination exploits the fact that ice formed from seawater excludes most of its salt. The practical difficulty is that freezing removes less energy per kilogram than evaporation but transfers it far more slowly, so crystalliser design and brine entrainment have kept the method out of commercial service for more than a century of attempts. Energy and cost The thermodynamic minimum work of separating seawater at 35,000 mg/L into pure water and brine is about 1.06 kWh per cubic metre. Real plants sit two to four times above that floor, and the gap is where engineering lives. Reverse osmosis has closed the gap faster than any thermal alternative, which is why it now accounts for roughly 69 percent of global contracted desalination capacity. Electricity price shapes plant design more than membrane price does. A plant paying 0.03 US dollars per kilowatt-hour can profitably run at high recovery and accept a larger brine stream; the same plant at 0.15 per kilowatt-hour will trade recovery for pressure-exchanger efficiency and may add photovoltaic capacity to shave the daytime peak. Saudi Arabia's Sakaka plant and the Al Khafji solar hybrid in the kingdom were built around that arithmetic. Intake and outfall works are a second, often underestimated cost line. Beach wells avoid much of the pretreatment burden but yield less water; open intakes need screen designs that do not entrain larvae, and the diffuser that returns concentrate must be long enough to reach a mixing zone where salinity returns to background within regulatory distance. For a 100,000 cubic metre per day plant those civil works can approach a third of capital cost. Environmental effects The concentrate
…
the conservation benefit in water-stressed regions that also suffer heat stress. Coupling plants to renewable generation or waste heat is therefore an environmental measure, not only a cost measure. Geographic distribution About half of installed capacity sits in the Middle East and North Africa, where groundwater depletion, flat terrain and oil revenue combine to make desalination the default supply option for coastal cities. Spain is the largest European operator, with the Canary Islands and the south-east coast depending on reverse osmosis for between 15 and 40 percent of municipal supply. The United States is concentrated in Florida, Texas and California, where brackish groundwater desalination now outpaces seawater in new permits. Small island states use desalination as insurance against drought rather than as a base-load source. Plants on Malta, Barbados and Singapore run at high utilisation, and Singapore's hybrid system couples reverse osmosis with reclaimed water and rainwater capture so that no single source can fail the city. That portfolio logic, rather than any single technology, is the pattern most often copied. Installed desalination capacity by region Region Share of capacity Installed (million m3/day) Dominant process Middle East and North Africa 47% 18.6 thermal and RO Asia-Pacific 19% 7.4 RO and brackish Europe 16% 6.3 RO Americas 14% 5.5 brackish RO Sub-Saharan Africa 4% 1.6 RO, modular Notable plants The plants listed below are included because they illustrate a design choice: heat co-location in Saudi Arabia, solar hybridisation in Algeria, modular expansion in Australia, or a record-low power draw in Israel. Output figures are nameplate capacity at commissioning and do not always match later operating data. Largest and most-cited desalination plants Plant Country Process Capacity (m3/day) Commissioned Ras Al Khair Saudi Arabia MSF / RO 1,036,000 2014 Sorek Israel RO 624,000 2013 Taweelah United Arab Emirates RO 909,200 2022 Carlsbad United States RO 190,000 2015 Perth Southern Seawater Australia RO 500,000 2011 Sakaka Saudi Arabia RO 60,000 2021 Social and political context Desalination is often framed as a technical fix, but access is allocated politically. In several coastal cities piped desalinated water reaches new developments while older neighbourhoods remain on intermittent tankers, because the distribution network, not the pla
…
ies split the bill into a volumetric rate that covers production and a fixed service charge that covers the plant's capital cost, which keeps low-volume households from subsidising large landscapers. Water quality and health Desalinated water is almost distilled in its mineral content, which raises two practical questions. First, it can be corrosive to distribution pipes because it has little buffering capacity; utilities stabilise it by adding calcium hydroxide or carbon dioxide before it leaves the plant, a step called remineralisation. Second, very soft water has been associated with lower intakes of calcium and magnesium, though the health evidence is observational and contested. Disinfection by-products form when chlorine reacts with the small amount of natural organic matter that survives reverse osmosis. Because product water is low in organic carbon, plants typically maintain a free chlorine residual through the network rather than relying on chloramination, which can decay in dead ends. Regulatory frameworks in the European Union and the United States set separate limits for boron and bromate, both of which are concentrated in the feed and only partially rejected by the membrane. Boron is the ion that most often forces a second pass. It exists as uncharged boric acid at seawater pH, so a single reverse osmosis stage rejects only about 70 to 85 percent of it. Raising the pH to 9 or 10 converts boron to the borate ion, which the membrane rejects far better, but the second pass then needs its own pressure and its own energy recovery loop. Plants serving irrigation in boron-sensitive crops, such as citrus and stone fruit, are the ones that routinely pay for that second pass. Nitrates and pharmaceutical residues in brackish feed are a different problem again. Reverse osmosis rejects both well, but the concentrate carries them into the outfall, so a plant that cleans a river for drinking can still return micropollutants to the same river downstream. Advanced oxidation before the membrane or activated carbon after it are the usual answers, and both add a chemical cost line that rarely appears in the headline price per cubic metre. Small-scale and emergency systems Containerised reverse osmosis units have become the standard response after hurricanes and earthquakes. A 40-foot container can hold a complete train, including pretreatment, membrane racks, a di
…
containers sitting unopened because the receiving country could not supply the last two. Capacity pledges that do not include an operating budget are closer to public relations than to water supply. Future directions Three research threads are likely to matter over the next decade. The first is brine valorisation: extracting magnesium, lithium and calcium from concentrate so that the outfall becomes a mineral product. Pilot crystallisers already recover magnesium hydroxide at grades that sell into flame-retardant and wastewater markets, though lithium recovery from seawater remains far below the concentration needed for economic extraction. The second is low-energy membranes, including biomimetic aquaporin channels and graphene oxide laminates. Aquaporin-based hollow fibres have reached pilot scale in Denmark and show salt rejection above 99.5 percent at pressures close to osmotic, but manufacturing reproducibility and chlorine tolerance are unresolved. The third is demand-side integration. Plants that can ramp with solar output, charge raised reservoirs during the day and draw them at night turn desalination from a constant load into a grid flexibility asset. Western Australia's Perth plants already follow that pattern with dedicated wind and solar farms, and the model is spreading to Chile and Namibia. None of these directions removes the fundamental trade: freshwater from seawater is bought with energy, and the only durable way to lower the price is to lower the energy per cubic metre or to waste less of the water once it reaches the tap. Both levers are cheaper than building another plant. See also Related articles cover the supply side and the demand side of the same question. Water reuse describes the alternative of treating wastewater to a potable standard, which in several cities has proved cheaper than moving seawater uphill; managed aquifer recharge describes storing wet-season water underground so that pumping can stop during droughts.
